To know permissions in bash shell

Warning: on Windows, the behavior of chmod depends on the console used. For instance, using MINGW64, changing the mode of a file will depend on the shebang: no shebang -> chmod does not work; #! -> chmod works. With WSL2, no problem detected for chmod. chmod change the rights for a file or a directory Examples: chmod +x file1 autorize execution only for me chmod +x dir1/ autorize execution only for me for all the files inside the directory dir1 chmod -R +x dir1/ autorize execution only for me for all the files and subdirectories inside the directory dir1 chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o=r file1 The letters u, g, and o stand for "user", "group", and "other". The equals sign ("=") means "set the permissions exactly like this," and the letters "r", "w", and "x" stand for "read", "write", and "execute", respectively. The commas separate the different classes of permissions, and there are no spaces in between them. chmod -R 700 dir1/ recover read write exe of dir1 and subdir only for me. In case of right loss, try: chmod u+rwX dir1/ autorize execution only for me for all the files and subdirectories inside the directory dir1 Numbers can be used for "user", "group", and "other", like this: 0 = no permissions whatsoever; this person cannot read, write, or execute the file 1 = execute only 2 = write only 3 = write and execute (1+2) 4 = read only 5 = read and execute (4+1) 6 = read and write (4+2) 7 = read and write and execute (4+2+1) Example: 777 means read and write and execute for "user", "group", and "other". Of note: to move a file using mv requires write permission. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chmod

https://www.cyberciti.biz/faq/creating-soft-link-or-symbolic-link/ A symbolic link is a file that point toward another "real" file. This avoids the duplication of files on a computer. Two kinds: soft and hard. Soft: files that point to the "real" file are abstractions. If the "real" file is removed, the connection is lost. Hard: the "real" file has two entries in the inode table. Hard links are problematic. If one want to remove a big file that has several entries in the inode table, it will not be erased and it is not easy to find the different entries of a file. Thus avoid hard links. To create a soft symbolic link: ln -s file1 link1 # -s for soft (beware ln by default is hard), file1 is the source file to point The color of the pointing path depends on the rights of the pointed file. Example: Red: the pointed file does not exists (check the path) or has no execution rigths Green: pointed file with execution right Grey: pointed file with no execution right Cyan: point toward a directory T To remove a symbolic link: unlink file1 # it seems that unlink link1 also works Warning: 1) Always use symbolic links for files, not for directories. With files, there is no possible way to accidentally delete the target of a symbolic link using rm. 2) Never use rm -r on large directories if it is or if it contains directory symbolic link because can delete the content of the pointed directory (target). Use ls -lR <PATH> | grep ^l to know if there are symbolic links in a folder Example from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62637046/how-to-make-rm-not-delete-symbolic-links $ mkdir test1 $ touch test1/foo.txt $ ln -s test1 test2 $ ls -lR .: total 4 drwxrwxr-x 2 soren soren 4096 Jun 29 17:02 test1 lrwxrwxrwx 1 soren soren 5 Jun 29 17:02 test2 -> test1 ./test1: total 0 -rw-rw-r-- 1 soren soren 0 Jun 29 17:02 foo.txt These are all safe: rm test2 (deletes the symlink only) rm -r test2 (deletes the symlink only) rm -rf test2 (deletes the symlink only) rm test2/ (rm: cannot remove 'test2/': Is a directory -- no action taken) rm -rf *2 (or any other glob matching the symlink -- deletes the symlink only) These are not safe: rm -r test2/ (rm: cannot remove 'test2/': Not a directory -- but deletes the contents of the test1 directory) rm -rf test2/ (deletes the contents of the directory, leaves the symlink, no error) rm -rf test2/* (deletes the contents of the directory, leaves the symlink, no error) To copy the target of a symbolic link, and not the link file: cp -L link1 https://stackoverflow.com/questions/27870965/linux-cp-how-to-have-it-follow-links-but-not-stop-if-a-link-target-doesnt-exis To replace a symlink file by the hard file: shopt -s globstar sed -i '' **/* # **/* is a bash globstar pattern meaning "all files and all folders, at all depth, from here" To detect all the symlinks in a folder: find . -xtype l | while read -r symlink ; do echo $symlink done To change all the broken paths of sym files in a folder (gpt5): #!/usr/bin/env bash # Set the paths old="/pasteur/appa/scratch/gmillot" new="/pasteur/helix/projects/project_b/results" # Find broken symlinks find . -xtype l | while read -r link ; do target=$(readlink "$link") # Only adjust if target starts with the old path if [[ $target == $old* ]]; then newtarget="${target/$old/$new}" echo "Updating: $link" echo " from: $target" echo " to: $newtarget" # Remove the old symlink and create the updated one rm "$link" ln -s "$newtarget" "$link" fi done Of, note: readlink reports what a symlink points to. ln -sfn safely forces the link to point to the new target. find ... -type l lists only symlinks; -maxdepth 1 keeps it to the given folder (remove if you want recursion). The if [[ "$target" == $old_prefix* ]] ensures only links with the old path are updated. • find . -xtype l finds broken symlinks in current dir and subdirs. • readlink "$link" gets the symlink’s target.

Glob pattern in file names or path
Glob pattern in file names or path is not regex, it is called "extended globbing" or "wildcard".

https://www.linuxjournal.com/content/bash-extended-globbing https://www.gnu.org/software/make/manual/html_node/Wildcard-Function.html https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/essential/io/fileOps.html#glob An asterisk, *, matches any number of characters (including none). Two asterisks, **, works like * but crosses directory boundaries. This syntax is generally used for matching complete paths. A question mark, ?, matches exactly one character. Braces specify a collection of subpatterns. For example: {sun,moon,smaestro} matches "sun", "moon", or "smaestro". {temp*,tmp*} matches all strings beginning with "temp" or "tmp". Square brackets convey a set of single characters or, when the hyphen character (-) is used, a range of characters. For example: [aeiou] matches any lowercase vowel. [0-9] matches any digit. [A-Z] matches any uppercase letter. [a-z,A-Z] matches any uppercase or lowercase letter. Within the square brackets, *, ?, and \ match themselves. All other characters match themselves. To match *, ?, or the other special characters, you can escape them by using the backslash character, \. For example: \\ matches a single backslash, and \? matches the question mark. Here are some examples of glob syntax: *.html – Matches all strings that end in .html ??? – Matches all strings with exactly three letters or digits *[0-9]* – Matches all strings containing a numeric value *.{htm,html,pdf} – Matches any string ending with .htm, .html or .pdf a?*.java – Matches any string beginning with a, followed by at least one letter or digit, and ending with .java {foo*,*[0-9]*} – Matches any string beginning with foo or any string containing a numeric value Note: If you are typing the glob pattern at the keyboard and it contains one of the special characters, you must put the pattern in quotes ("*"), use the backslash (\*), or use whatever escape mechanism is supported at the command line.

https://www.linuxjournal.com/content/return-values-bash-functions Bash functions, unlike functions in most programming languages do not allow you to return a value to the caller. When a bash function ends its return value is its status: zero for success, non-zero for failure. To return values, you can set a global variable with the result, or use command substitution, or you can pass in the name of a variable to use as the result variable. The examples below describe these different mechanisms. Although bash has a return statement, the only thing you can specify with it is the function's status, which is a numeric value like the value specified in an exit statement. The status value is stored in the $? variable. If a function does not contain a return statement, its status is set based on the status of the last statement executed in the function. To actually return arbitrary values to the caller you must use other mechanisms. The simplest way to return a value from a bash function is to just set a global variable to the result. Since all variables in bash are global by default this is easy: function myfunc() { myresult='some value' } myfunc echo $myresult The code above sets the global variable myresult to the function result. Reasonably simple, but as we all know, using global variables, particularly in large programs, can lead to difficult to find bugs. A better approach is to use local variables in your functions. The problem then becomes how do you get the result to the caller. One mechanism is to use command substitution: function myfunc() { local myresult='some value' echo "$myresult" } result=$(myfunc) # or result=`myfunc` echo $result Here the result is output to the stdout and the caller uses command substitution to capture the value in a variable. The variable can then be used as needed.

Notion of mutable and immutable objects

This notion is linked to the memory location of objects. Immutable objects are objects for which the memory location is changed if a element is changed in the object. Type of immutable objects: int, float, bool, str, tuple, unicode Mutable objects are objects for which the memory location is not changed if a element is changed in the object. Type of mutable objects: list, set, dict. Example of immutable object: i = 1 # type integer id(i) # id() provide the memory location # ***704 i += 1 # element of i is changed i 2 id(i) # memory location is changed # ***736 (different from ***704) Example of mutable object: x = ['a', 'b', 'c'] # list x id(x) # 68320520 x[1] = 4 # second element of the list is changed x id(x) # memory location not changed # 68320520 The strong benefit of mutable objects that modifing a mutable object is faster, notably when objects are big or complex. Indeed, for large and/or complex objects, creating a new copy of the object for every single change can be very costly and/or tedious. And for objects with a distinct identity, changing an existing objects is much more simple and intuitive than creating a new, modified copy of it.

A Dockerfile is the recipe file for docker. Must have this format (FROM, RUN, etc., see section Main commands): # base image: Ubuntu FROM ubuntu:16.04 RUN apt-get update --fix-missing \ # update apt-get && apt-get install -y git make g++ zlib1g-dev \ # install the dependencies git make g++ zlib1g-dev && cd /usr/local/ \ && git clone https://github.com/OpenGene/fastp.git \ # clone fastp && cd fastp \ && make \ && make install \ && cd /usr/local \ && rm -rf fastp \ && apt-get remove -y git make g++ zlib1g-dev \ # important to remove the dependencies after installation to save space in the image that will be built && apt-get autoremove -y \ && apt-get clean \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/fastp"] # run fastp when this image is run (exec mode writing) To create a dockerfile, goes into: C:\Users\gael\Documents\Git_projects\dockerfiles And create a new fastp file. Then copy-paste the code above into that file. And, from WSL2, copy the file into the linux environment cp /mnt/c/Users/Gael/Documents/Git_projects/dockerfiles/fastp /home/gael/dockerfiles/

Very important field as it can be inspected for certain fields using docker image inspect <myimage>. Several labels fields can be used. Use "\" to cut a string by a carriage return. Use quotes for spaces: LABEL version="1.0" LABEL image.description="This image \ is good" Or in a single field: LABEL version="1.0" \ image.description="This image \ is good" MAINTAINER deprecated. Use LABEL COPY adds files from your Docker client’s current directory RUN execute the following POSIX shell commands, i.e., builds your application with make. Use && and \ when using ends of line: \ to specify that the command is not finished and && to say that is is a continuation of a command. Warning: the language is not bash, it is POSIX shell, that, for instance, 1) does not support array but only single values, 2) does not like but , 3) does not like long string () CMD specifies what command to run within the container ENTRYPOINT before the entrypoint, all the code is only for the image creation. With entrypoint, it is possible to thenafter directly create the container and run some commands inside the container. Two forms: (1) the exec form ENTRYPOINT ["executable", "param1", "param2"] and the shell form ENTRYPOINT command param1 param2. The exec form is parsed as a JSON array, which means that you must use double-quotes (") around words not single-quotes ('). See https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/#entrypoint. Beware of the difference between the login shell and the classical login, since the login shell sources the files of the init system while the classical shell sources the files of the init user when the container is activated. Examples: ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/bash" , "-l"] for the former and ENTRYPOINT ["/bin/bash"] for the latter.

Running an image create a container and potentially run commands inside it. In such case the container remains closed. Depending on the options, it is also possible to open the container and be in the container environment with the system and soft inside of the corresponding image. Once opened, we can work inside it. Warning: opening an image to use a python session, for instance, can create problems of path, i.e., packages will not be found even if they are in the image because the container look into the locales packages, not into the container. To overcome this, open the image with --entrypoint bash and than open a python session.

-v Link your current directory to a directory with the same absolute path in the container. First path is from the host (local machine), second is the path inside the docker. If the second one does not exist, it is created directly. Example: -v /mnt/c/Users/:/tmp means that the tree starting at Users in the local system is mounted into /tmp in the container. Then, to call this folder C:\\Users\\gael\\Documents in the container, we have to write /tmp/gael/Documents --mount similar to -v ? Example: --mount "type=bind,src=/mnt/c/Users/Gael/,dst=/caca/" --entrypoint overwrite the entrypoint inside the image. Useful when the default entrypoint is R but we want to be in the ubuntu environment (hence --entrypoint bash) -i interactif TTY. Means that all the code is executed but after that, we stay in the container environment through a TTY (teletype writter, see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/43099116/error-the-input-device-is-not-a-tty) system. Warning we can do nothing without -t -t to have the TTY, i.e., to be able to write inside the container env. Madatory when using -i -w --workdir. Equivalent to a cd made once the container is opened. If the path does not exist in the container, it is created --rm close the container after running. Ohterwise, still in use (whatever the use of -ti or not) see also https://pandorafms.com/blog/docker-run/
docker run -v <PATH>:<PATH> --entrypoint bash -i -t <IMAGE_NAME>:<VERSION_NAME> Here --entrypoint bash -it just open the container.

Mounting a drive in a container using -v

Example: sudo docker run -v $PWD:$PWD -ti gmillot/bash-extended_v1.0:gitlab_v1.0 $PWD is the pwd displayed in the console before running the image. Here it means: 1) before the colon, mount that path inside the container and 2) after the colon, create inside the image a path (by creating all the intermediate directories) from the root that is $PWD. Thus, if PWD = /mnt/c/Users/Gael/Documents/Git_projects/project_a/, it means that this path is mounted into the container at this destination inside the container: /mnt/c/Users/Gael/Documents/Git_projects/project_a. This facilitate the use of script inside the container because it looks like the local folder Example: sudo docker run -v /mnt/c/Users/Gael/Documents/Git_projects/project_a/:/caca -ti --entrypoint bash 1e828c256ff0 Here /mnt/c/Users/Gael/Documents/Git_projects/project_a from the local machine is mounted into the /caca path inside the container. Warning: mounting a drive using -v does not work when this drive is a distant drive using WSL. Example: FOLDER="\\\helix.pasteur.fr\projects\BioIT\gmillot" sudo mkdir /mnt/share sudo mount -t drvfs "$FOLDER" /mnt/share sudo docker run -v /mnt/share/:/caca -ti --entrypoint bash gmillot/r_v4.1.2_extended_v2.1:gitlab_v8.8 Nothing is present in /caca. https://apptainer.org/docs/user/main/definition_files.html#definition-files A definition file has a header and a body. The header determines the base container to begin with. The body is further divided into sections that perform things like software installation, environment setup, and copying files into the container from host system, etc. Example: Bootstrap: library From: ubuntu:18.04 Stage: gael_build %setup touch /file1 touch ${APPTAINER_ROOTFS}/file2 %files /file1 /file1 /opt %environment export LISTEN_PORT=12345 export LC_ALL=C %post apt-get update && apt-get install -y netcat NOW=`date` echo "export NOW=\"${NOW}\"" >> $APPTAINER_ENVIRONMENT %runscript echo "Container was created $NOW" echo "Arguments received: $*" exec echo "$@" %startscript nc -lp $LISTEN_PORT %test grep -q NAME=\"Ubuntu\" /etc/os-release if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "Container base is Ubuntu as expected." else echo "Container base is not Ubuntu." exit 1 fi %labels Author d@sylabs.io Version v0.0.1 %help This is a demo container used to illustrate a def file that uses all supported sections. In this example, the header, made of Bootstrap, From and Stage, tells Apptainer to use a base Ubuntu 16.04 image from the Container Library. The stage section just names the section initiated by the header, since several headers (stages) can be in a single definition file. See https://apptainer.org/docs/user/main/definition_files.html#multi-stage-builds

The only keyword that is required for every type of build is Bootstrap. It determines the bootstrap agent that will be used to create the base operating system you want to use. For example, the library bootstrap agent will pull a container from the Container Library as a base. Similarly, the docker bootstrap agent will pull docker layers from Docker Hub as a base OS to start your image. Starting with Singularity 3.2, the Bootstrap keyword needs to be the first entry in the header section. This breaks compatibility with older versions that allow the parameters of the header to appear in any order. Preferred bootstrap agents: library images hosted on the Container Library docker images hosted on Docker Hub shub deprecated scratch a flexible option for building a container from scratch See https://apptainer.org/docs/user/main/definition_files.html#preferred-bootstrap-agents

%setup commands in this section are first executed on the host system outside of the container after the base OS has been installed. Warning: executed outside of the container on the host system itself, and is executed with elevated privileges. Can alter and potentially damage the host %file copy files into the container (greater safety than using the %setup section) %post execute within the container at build time after the base OS has been installed. The %post section is therefore the place to perform installations of new applications %environment defines some environment variables that will be available to the container at runtime %runscript this content is written to a file within the container that is executed when the container image is run (either via the singularity run command or by executing the container directly as a command) %test this section is run at the very end of the build process to validate the container %labels used to add metadata to the file /.singularity.d/labels.json within your container %help this section is transcribed into a metadata file in the container during the build. This text can then be displayed using the run-help command. See https://apptainer.org/docs/user/main/definition_files.html#sections

Running an image creates a container and potentially run commands inside it. In such cases the container remains closed. Depending on the options, it is also possible to open the container and be in the container environment with the system and soft inside of the corresponding image. Once opened, we can work inside it. To work in a container with bash: apptainer shell fastqc.img Difference between apptainer run and apptainer exec: apptainer run run the default command set for containers based on the specified image. This default command is set within the image metadata when the image is built. You do not specify a command to run when using apptainer run, you simply specify the image file name. As we saw earlier, you can use the apptainer inspect command to see what command is run by default when starting a new container based on an image. apptainer exec start a container based on the specified image and run the command provided on the command line following apptainer exec <image file name>. Very important to understand how nextflow works

The nextflow pipeline file are named by default main.nf. The nextflow config file must are named by default nextflow.config. It is possible to modify these two names. But it will not work if the idea is to work from a distant repository (see section Precision when running a distant nextflow file).

Nextflow create a folder for each process of the .nf file (or each parallelization of each process) in the work directory. For instance 00/5bf63033e13094f180fe69c583ce3c. Then, everything of the process is perform in this folder, which becomes the working environment (a kind of home). If INPUT is present, then files or values are imported. For the files, a symbolic link is created pointing to the initial file (in another folder of the work directory, or in a dataset folder). All the new files are created here. If publishDir is used, then the files referenced in OUTPUT are copy/paste into the designed publishDir folder. Execution files are also hosted here. Example in the work folder work/1c/8b95199cc174e6590288faf07f3658: .command.err : Content of STDERR .command.log : Log File (STDOUT+STDERR) .command.out : Content of STDOUT .command.run : Nextflow generated commands to run the script (cloud, etc.) .command.sh : Script of the task (“script:“ in process definition) .command.trace : Memory/CPU/Disk footprint of the task .exitcode : Exit status of the task

Warning, because of the symbolic links, every imported file that is modified by the process is not only modified in the work folder but also were the link point, meaning that initial input data can be modifed ! To prevent that : 1) always use input files that are "write" protected (read and execute only). 2) Copy the input file in the process before working: input: file fs script: """ cp ${fs} tempo.txt chmod 777 tempo.txt ... See also section Very important to understand for a better example of copy.

A strong advantage of nextflow is to rerun the pipeline using the -resume option of the run command. In such case, all the processes that are cache 'true' are not run but linked to the previous same process execution, which save lots of time ! However, all the variables of the .config used in the process must be declared in the input section of the process. Otherwise, nextflow will not rerun a cache 'true' process using a variable modified in the .config file.

The scope of a process is such that if a variable is not in the input section, it looks for variables in the working environment of nextflow, which has notably sourced the env{} environment of the config file. Thus, it is not mandatory to use the input section to declare variables. However, in that case, nextflow will not rerun a cache 'true' process using a variable modified in the .config file.
Always start a .nf script by: nextflow.enable.dsl=2 With value 1 or 2 depending on the desired DSL.

Thus if * corresponds to 8 names, 8 couples are formed. The data channel is an object a bit like a list, made of 8 compartments, one for each file name, each compartment having 3 values: a name (corresponding to *), and two file names (corresponding to *_1.fq.gz and *_2.fq.gz). To complete the answer a bit: any closure {} has the the implicit variable "it". {x->} has no implicit "it" variable, but an explicit "x". {->} has not implicit "it" variable and no explicit variable

See https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/channel.html#channel-types Queue channel : single use A queue channel is a non-blocking unidirectional FIFO queue which connects two processes or operators. A queue channel is usually created using a factory method such as a from, fromPath, etc. or chaining it with a channel operator such as map, flatMap, etc. Queue channels are also created by process output declarations using the into clause. The definition implies that the same queue channel cannot be used more than one time as process output and more than one time as process input. If you need to connect a process output channel to more than one process or operator use the into operator to create two (or more) copies of the same channel and use each of them to connect a separate process. Value channel : multiple use A value channel a.k.a. singleton channel by definition is bound to a single value and it can be read unlimited times without consuming its content. For this reason a value channel can be used as input by more than one process. A value channel is created using the value factory method or by operators returning a single value, such as first, last, collect, count, min, max, reduce, sum. Thus, a channel recovering a value via stdout will not be considered as value channel. A value channel is implicitly created by a process when an input specifies a simple value in the from clause. Moreover, a value channel is also implicitly created as output for a process whose inputs are only value channels.
See http://groovy-lang.org/groovy-dev-kit.html#_data_and_objects See section Variable scope for the scope of the variables in nextflow.

Variables are mostly vectors of one element. Example: x = 1 println x x = new java.util.Date() println x x = -3.1499392 println x x = false println x x = "Hi" println x Variable can also be defined in processes or in the nextflow script: y = 2 process foo { script: x = 1 """ echo $x $y """ } See section Variable scope for the scope of the variables.

See http://groovy-lang.org/groovy-dev-kit.html#Collections-Ranges A range is like a Python xrange type, i.e., a range of integers. See https://fr.wikiversity.org/wiki/Python/Les_types_de_base Example: def range = 5..8 // range is a name not a function. Def is not mandatory assert range.size() == 4 assert range.get(2) == 7 assert range[2] == 7

See http://groovy-lang.org/groovy-dev-kit.html#Collections-Lists A list is like a Python list type, i.e., an ordered collection of elements, but it seems that in groovy, they are of same mode. See https://fr.wikiversity.org/wiki/Python/Les_types_de_base Example: def list = [5, 6, 7, 8] // list is a name not a function. Def is not mandatory assert list.get(2) == 7 assert list[2] == 7 assert list instanceof java.util.List def emptyList = [] assert emptyList.size() == 0 emptyList.add(5) assert emptyList.size() == 1

See http://groovy-lang.org/groovy-dev-kit.html#Collections-Maps A map is like Python dictionnary type, i.e., an unordered collection of objects. See https://fr.wikiversity.org/wiki/Python/Les_types_de_base Example: def map = [name: 'Gromit', likes: 'cheese', id: 1234] assert map.get('name') == 'Gromit' assert map.get('id') == 1234 assert map['name'] == 'Gromit' assert map['id'] == 1234 assert map instanceof java.util.Map def emptyMap = [:] assert emptyMap.size() == 0 emptyMap.put("foo", 5) assert emptyMap.size() == 1 assert emptyMap.get("foo") == 5

See https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/process.html#output-tuple-of-values A tuple is like Python tuple type, i.e., an unordered collection of objects. See https://fr.wikiversity.org/wiki/Python/Les_types_de_base The tuple qualifier allows you to send multiple values into a single channel. This feature is useful when you need to group together the results of multiple executions of the same process, as shown in the following example: query_ch = Channel.fromPath '*.fa' species_ch = Channel.from 'human', 'cow', 'horse' process blast { input: val query from query_ch file species from species_ch output: tuple val(species), file('result') into blastOuts script: """ blast -db nr -query $query > result """ } In the above example a BLAST task is executed for each pair of species and query that are received. When the task completes a new tuple containing the value for species and the file result is sent to the blastOuts channel.

Pipeline parameters are simply declared by prepending to a variable name the prefix params, separated by dot character. Their value can be specified on the command line by prefixing the parameter name with a double dash character, i.e. --paramName. As an example, here is what should be written in the main.nf file: params.str = 'Hello world!' Which is used like this: nextflow run tutorial.nf --str 'Bonjour le monde' The string specified on the command line will override the default value of the parameter. As of version 20.11.0-edge any . (dot) character in a parameter name is interpreted as the delimiter or nested scope e.g. --foo.bar Hello will be accessible from the script as params.foo.bar. If you want to have a parameter name including a . (dot) character escape it using the back-slash character e.g. --foo\.bar Hello the variable can be used as it is in the nextflow script: ${params.str} Or reassigned in a more easy readable variable: str=params.str

A process is a section of a nf script that processes channels or variables. The definition is: process <name> { } Between the brackets is what is called the body of the process. The minimal structure is: process <NAME> { <user script of the required task> } But it is better to name the execution block using script, shell or exec: process <NAME> { [script | shell | exec]: <user script of the required task> } Can start with directives as publishDir. And then is made of blocks, like: input: input output: output when: when execute the task script | shell | exec: task to execute If the channel has several values, the process is parallelized. Full structure : process < name > { [ directives ] input: < process inputs > output: < process outputs > when : < condition > [ script| shell| exec ]: < user script to be executed > }

Nextflow first check if the variable is present 1) in the script of the execution block of a process, 2) in the execution block of a process, but before the script, 3) in the channel, then in the nextflow script, and then in the system ($PATH for instance). Single quotes in the execution block scoops the scope and goes directly into the system environment if the variable is not defined between the quotes. See https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/process.html#script. Example: copy-paste the following code into the file /mnt/c/Users/Gael/Desktop/caca.nf x=4 process A { x=3 # variable cannot be defined inside process but outside of the execution block output: "res.txt" script: x=2 """ x=1 echo "Result is:" \$x > res.txt # if $x is used, it is replaced during the writting into the work/.../.command.sh file before execution of this file """ } And execute: nextflow run caca.nf Check the result in work/.../res.txt Then, play with inactivation and \$x to see the scope: # x=1 echo "Result is:" \$x > res.txt -> Error: because the .command.sh has no variable x defined. echo "Result is:" $x > res.txt With no inactivation, the replacement of $x is performed before the writing of .command.sh, and the result is 2. //x=2 echo "Result is:" $x > res.txt With //x=2, the replacement of $x is performed before the writing of .command.sh, and the result is 4, because a ariable cannot be defined inside process but outside of the execution block. //x=4 //x=2 echo "Result is:" $x > res.txt -> Error: because during the .command.sh writing, no variable x is defined, and the fact to use: x=5 nextflow run caca.nf Does not work either. Now using single quotes: ''' x=1 echo "Result is:" $x > res.txt ''' The result is 1. ''' # x=1 echo "Result is:" $x > res.txt ''' -> Error: because during the .command.sh writing, the scope is impaired by the single quotes. ''' # x=1 echo "Result is:" $PATH > res.txt ''' The $PATH system variable is returned.

When a process is run, a working directory is created (inside the general working directory known thanks to the workDir implicit variable) and all the files declared in the input block are added into this directory thanks to symbolic links. For instance, when the process configBackup in C:\Users\gael\Documents\Git_projects\project_a\main.nf is run (see section Backup the nextflow.config file into the result folder): config_file = workflow.configFiles[0] // better to use this than config_file = file("${projectDir}/ig_clustering.config") because the latter is not good if -c option of nextflow run is used result_folder_name="20210903_res_project_a" out_path="/mnt/c/Users/Gael/Desktop" out_path="${out_path}/${result_folder_name}" process configBackup { publishDir "${out_path}", mode: 'copy', overwrite: false input: file config_file output: file "${config_file}" // warning message if we use file config_file script: // mandatory block """ """ } The directory work\b0\2f59852ea304ebe335edfdf3fd9d68 is created and the file config_file (which is by default "${projectDir}/nextflow.config" except if -c option of nextflow run is used) is, added, using a symbolic link (warning: not seen through Windows OS windows): Now if: 1) publishDir "${out_path}" is used at the beginning of the process 2) a file is present in the input block 3) and also present in the output block Then, the file is copied into the publishDir folder using a symbolic link (warning: not seen through Windows OS windows): Now if in (1) publishDir "${out_path}", mode: 'copy' is used at the beginning of the process, then the file is copied hard into the publishDir folder: Now if in (1) publishDir "${out_path}", mode: 'copy' overwrite: false is used at the beginning of the process, then the file is copied into the publishDir folder according to the mode, but only if the file is not already in the publishDir folder, whatever the form. If an input file is modified in a process, we could imagine than only the file present in the work directory is modified. But due to the symbolic link, the initial file will be also modified. To prevent this: - NEVER modify a file using the same name. always change the mane of the modified file. - ALWAYS copy these files in the process that modifies the file, not in another process (to optimize the -resume option of nextflow run).

https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/process.html#directives publishDir where to publish the output files. Example: publishDir "${results}/", mode: 'copy' cache store the process results to a local cache. When the cache is enabled and the pipeline is launched with the -resume option, any following attempt to execute the process, along with the same inputs, will cause the process execution to be skipped, producing the stored data as the actual results. Example: cache 'false'. The 'deep' or 'lenient' value can be used instead of 'true' or 'false'. See https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/process.html?highlight=deep#cache executor where processes are executed. By default a process uses the executor defined globally in the nextflow.config file. Example: executor 'local' tag associate each process execution with a custom label, so that it will be easier to identify them in the log file or in the trace execution report. Example: tag "${name}" label connect the current process with the withLabel: . Example: label 'bwa'

See https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/process.html#publishdir. The publishDir directive copies output files of the output block into a folder. Example: publishDir path: "/mnt/c/Users/Gael/Desktop/", mode: 'copy', overwrite: false output: file "aligned.gz" into tempo_ch The aligned.gz file is sent into the tempo_ch channel but is also copied into the /mnt/c/Users/Gael/Desktop/ folder thanks to the publishDir directive. To get several output in folders (not into channels), use publishDir: publishDir path: "${results}/08_POS_QC", mode: 'link', pattern: 'out_*/*' // for the output result of pos_qc into 08_POS_QC publishDir path: "${results}/", mode: 'link', pattern: 'Full_Results.tsv' // for the copy of Full_Results.tsv from 08_POS_QC into ${results}/ output: file "out_${vocqcfilename}*/*"// for the output result of voc_qc into 08_POS_QC file "Full_Results.tsv" // for the copy of Full_Results.tsv from 08_POS_QC into ${results}/ Parameters mode The file publishing method. See the following table for possible values. overwrite When true any existing file in the specified folder will be overridden (default: true during normal pipeline execution and false when pipeline execution is resumed). pattern Specifies a glob file pattern that selects which files to publish from the overall set of output files. See https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/essential/io/fileOps.html#glob path Specifies the directory where files need to be published. Note: the syntax publishDir '/some/dir' is a shortcut for publishDir path: '/some/dir'. saveAs A closure which, given the name of the file being published, returns the actual file name or a full path where the file is required to be stored. This can be used to rename or change the destination directory of the published files dynamically by using a custom strategy. Return the value null from the closure to not publish a file. This is useful when the process has multiple output files, but you want to publish only some of them. enabled Enable or disable the publish rule depending on the boolean value specified (default: true).

https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/process.html#inputs Warning: only channels can be specified in this block, even is it is not specified by "from" (which means in that case that the input name is the same as the channel name). Warning: it is possible to use variables in the script block that does not come from a channel (see section Variable scope). But not recommanded, notably to benefit from the -resume option if cache 'true'. Indeed, if a variable is modified, the -resume option + cache 'true' will not detect it and will rerun the process. Warning: a list in the input block, example methods = ['prot','dna', 'rna', 23, y] process foo { input: val x from methods results in a script run for each element of the list, independently. The parallelized processes are isolated from the others. Warning: a list of files in the input block for which we would except a parallelization, is not parallelized if another input has a unique file: only one of the files is processed. input: val file_name // a single variable file bam from dup_ch.mix(bowtie2_ch, q20_ch) // mix of three channels, i.e., three files in that case file "report.rmd" from log_ch14.first() // a single file in log_ch14 In this example, the three channels dup_ch, bowtie2_ch and q20_ch are assembled into a single one. The file_name variable is single but has no influence on the parallized process. However, report.rmd is a single file. If written as file "report.rmd" from log_ch14, the process takes only one of the three files from dup_ch.mix(bowtie2_ch, q20_ch) for the process. The first() operator is a trick to let nextflow believe that there are three files in log_ch14, which allow the parallelization. Warning, at that stage, the single report.rmd file are in three channels. In addition, the printing of the process shows that only one process is performed, while in fact 3. (See the .nextflow.log for the path of the three parallelized process). Thus, the first() strategy is not recommanded. It is better to have a correct definition of the parallelization. Nextflow processes are isolated from each other but can communicate between themselves sending values through channels. The input block defines from which channels the process expects to receive data. You can only define one input block at a time and it must contain one or more input declarations. The input block follows the syntax shown below: input: <input qualifier> <input name> from <source channel> [attributes] Example: Input: file tempo1 from file1 Input qualifier Declares the type of data to be received val take the channel as values env take the channel to set an environment variable named as the specified input name file take the channel as a file, staging it properly in the execution context path take the channel as a path, staging the file properly in the execution context stdin forward the channel to the process stdin special file tuple take the channel as a group of input values having one of the above qualifiers each lets you execute the process for each entry in the input collection Input name variable that will contain the data from the channel source channel Name of the channel to use. Must be preceeded by the keyword "from". attribute input optional attributes. Example ? Example num = Channel.from(1, 2, 3) process basicExample { input: val x from num script: "echo process job $x" } The val function takes each value of the num channel and put it into the x variable. Note that the results are in the .command.out of different folders, because the process is parallelized: \\wsl$\Ubuntu-20.04\home\gael\work\cf\8b0dc7603a6b28d7cd4da6e07befb9 When the input name is the same as the channel name, the from part of the declaration can be omitted: num = Channel.from(1, 2, 3) process basicExample { input: val num script: "echo process job $num" } Of note, possible to use several channels as input: num = Channel.from(1, 2, 3) time = Channel.from(5) process basicExample { input: val num val tempo from time.first() shell: """ echo '$num * $tempo' """ Warning: if num is made of several values, while ref is made of only one, but that both have to be used in the process, .first() has to be used. Warning with the scope of nextflow (see section Variable scope). Examples: num=Channel.from(5) x=4 process A { input: val x from num output: "res.txt" script: x=2 """ x=1 echo "Result is:" $x > res.txt # if $x is used, it is replaced during the writting into the work/.../.command.sh file before execution of this file """ } num=Channel.from(5) x=4 process A { input: val x from num output: "res.txt" script: //x=2 """ x=1 echo "Result is:" $x > res.txt # if $x is used, it is replaced during the writting into the work/.../.command.sh file before execution of this file """ } The result is 5, because the channel comes before the x=4 in the scope. With tuples: dsrc=Channel.fromFilePairs(params.fastq+'/*_R{1,2}.fastq.dsrc', flat: true) process dsrc2gz { label 'dsrc' input: tuple val(name), file(r1), file(r2) from dsrc The dsrc channel is an object a bit like a list, made of 8 compartments, one for each file name, each compartment having 3 values: a name (corresponding to *), and two file names (corresponding to *_1.fq.gz and *_2.fq.gz) With repeated inputs: https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/process.html#input-repeaters With fasta files: input: set id, seqString from fasta_ch.splitFasta(record:[header: true, seqString: true]) // warning: several data -> parall expected splitFasta(record:[header: true, seqString: true]) split a fasta files in records (one per sequence), each record with two items: the first is the header and the second the seq string. See https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/operator.html#splitfasta set takes the first and second items of the record

https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/process.html#outputs Warning: it is not possible to send a variable, a value, string, etc., from a complex script into channels. Only files works. The only way to get a variable is if the script return a single thing, which can be capted by the stdout qualifier. Warning: to get an output file of a script into a result directory, we must 1) declare the output file into the output block (whatever sent into a channel or not), and 2) use the publishDir directive (see section Directives). Warning: if an an output file of a script is not declared in the output block, it will never be present in the result directory. If it is present in the output block, it will depend of what is written in the publishDir directive. The output declaration block allows you to define the channels used by the process to send out the results produced. You can only define one output block at a time and it must contain one or more output declarations. The output block follows the syntax shown below: output: <output qualifier> <output name> into <target channel>[,channel,..] [attribute [,..]] If not into used, a channel with the same name is created (as for the input block) and is useable. Example: Output: file "example1.txt" into tempo2,tempo3 Several channels can be created here Global pattern can be used to specify several file names (see protocol 44): Output: file "{head,table}*.txt" into tempo2 Output qualifier Declares the type of data to be received val send variables with the name specified over the output channel env send a file defined in the process environment with the name specified over the output channel file send a file produced by the process with the name specified over the output channel path idem file stdout send the executed process stdout over the output channel tuple send multiple values over the same output channel Output name variable that will be sent into the channel target channel Name of the channel to use. Must be preceeded by the keyword "into". attribute output optional attributes. Example ? Example num = Channel.from(1, 2, 3) process basicExample { input: val x from num output: val x into tempo script: """ echo $x > file """ } See section Input. Of note, when the output name is the same as the channel name, the into part of the declaration can be omitted. Several channels can be defined: output: val x into var_channel val 'BB11' into str_channel val "${fasta.baseName}.out" into exp_channel Another way to declare several outputs: output: file "${fq.baseName}_fastqc.*" // fq.baseName means the base name of the input file named fq // .* means that all the fastqc.* files will be printed if publishDir is declared Example with tuple: file1 = Channel.fromPath("covid.fa") process indexRef { input: file x from file1 output: tuple val(x.Name), file("${x.baseName}.*") into tempo2 script: """ bwa index ${x} """ } val(x.Name) take the name of the variable x that is a file, and take it as character using val() See also https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/script.html#check-file-attributes where: x.getName() or x.Name Gets the file name e.g. /some/path/file.txt -> file.txt x.getBaseName() or x.BaseName Gets the file name without its extension e.g. /some/path/file.tar.gz -> file.tar x.getSimpleName() or x.SimpleName Gets the file name without any extension e.g. /some/path/file.tar.gz -> file To get several output in folders (not into channels), use publishDir: publishDir "${results}/08_POS_QC", mode: 'link', pattern: 'out_*/*' // for the output result of pos_qc into 08_POS_QC publishDir "${results}/", mode: 'link', pattern: 'Full_Results.tsv' // for the copy of Full_Results.tsv from 08_POS_QC into ${results}/ output: file "out_${vocqcfilename}*/*"// for the output result of voc_qc into 08_POS_QC file "Full_Results.tsv" // for the copy of Full_Results.tsv from 08_POS_QC into ${results}/

https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/process.html A process contains one and only one script or shell or exec block, and it must be the last statement when the process contains input and output declarations. The entered string is executed as a Bash script in the host system. It can be any command, script or combination of them, that you would normally use in terminal shell or in a common Bash script.

1) If a script file is used in this block, it must be inside the ./bin/ folder if main.nf is in ./ 2) Whatever the entrypoint declared in a docker or singularity image used in a process, the code written in the script section is considered by default as bash. Thus, always specify the shebang at the beginning of the process. Example: script: """ #!/bin/bash -ue echo "Hello" """ 3) When using files to run in the script section, located in the ./bin folder, always precise the executing file to use with the shebang. Example with a .R file. The script section is: script: """ #!/bin/bash -ue tree_vizu.R \ "${tree_kind}" \ "tree_vizu.log" """ and the beginning of the tree_vizu.R file is: #!/usr/bin/Rscript We can also use the absolute path of the executing file: script: """ #!/bin/bash -ue /usr/bin/Rscript -e ' cat("Hello") ' """ 4) When using Rscript in the script section, do not forget to use -e: script: """ #!/bin/bash -ue /usr/bin/Rscript -e ' cat("Hello") ' """ 5) It is possible to use variables that are not declared in the input block. But not recommanded, notably to help the -resume option if cache 'true' (it might be possible that the -resume option check the modifications of variables in channel but not other variables ?). 6) The number of character must not be too long in that section. Otherwise, weird messages can appear (see section Weird message (with process run but no output)). 7) Every messages and warnings coming from this section are not displayed in the executing window. Only error are returned by nextflow. The other messages are in the .command.log and .command.out files, in the work folder of the process: If messages are required, either assign to a log folder and use publishDir (section publishDir) or use instruction in groovy inside workflow{}: parseDb_filtering.out.unproductive_ch.count().subscribe{ n -> if ( n == 0 ){ print "

WARNING: EMPTY unproductive_seq.tsv FILE RETURNED FOLLOWING THE parseDb_filtering PROCESS

" }else{ it -> it.copyTo("${out_path}/unproductive_seq.tsv") } } 8) The use of |& tee -a file.log prevents the arrest of the nextflow execution and error message display. Example : script: """ if [[ "${meta_file}" != "NULL" && "${meta_legend}" != "NULL" ]] ; then Rscript -e ' df <- read.table("${file_assembly_ch}", header = TRUE, sep = "\t") meta <- read.table("${meta_file}", header = TRUE, sep = "\t") if(names(meta)[1] != "Label"){ stop(paste0("\n\n============\n\nERROR IN THE metadata_check PROCESS OF NEXTFLOW\nIF THE meta_path PARAMETER IS NOT \"NULL\", THEN THE FIRST COLUMN OF THE METADATA FILE MUST BE NAMED \"Label\" AND BE MADE OF THE NAMES OF THE FASTA SEQUENCES\n\n============\n\n"), call. = FALSE) } ' |& tee -a file_assembly.log fi """ With such script section, the error message is printed into the file_assembly.log file, but not in the console. And the process is not interrupted. Removing |& tee -a file_assembly.log solves the problem.

Kind of language Bash by default. Example of language modification num = Channel.from(1, 2, 3) time = Channel.from(5) process basicExample { input: val num val tempo from time.first() script: """ #!/usr/bin/python3 print(\"the result is \" + str($num + $tempo)) """ } Variable evaluation No nextflow variable evaluation and single line -> single quote or triple single quote. Example: 'echo The path is: $PATH' ''' echo The path is: $PATH ''' In this example PATH is not subtituted before sending the script to bash (default). No nextflow variable evaluation and multiple lines -> triple single quote. Example: ''' echo The path is: $PATH echo "Hello world" ''' Nextflow variable evaluation and single line -> double quote or triple double quote. Example: "echo The path is: $PATH" """ echo The path is: $PATH """ In this example, if PATH is a nextflow variable (defined in the input section of the process, or before the process) it is substituted before sending the script to bash (default). Nextflow variable evaluation and multiple lines -> triple double quote. Example: """ echo The path is: $PATH echo \"Hello world\" """ Here, the quotes inside the script are inactivated using \. Another example """ echo -e The path is:\\n$PATH """ Here, the \n inside the script is inactivated using \. Full example num = Channel.from(1, 2, 3) process basicExample { input: val num script: """ #!/usr/bin/bash echo \"The result is \$(( $num * 5 ))\" """ } The shebang is used to force the execution using bash (another language can be used like this). The $ of num is not inactivated because we need the variable substitution before sending the code to bash. However, the $(( has to be inactivated using \, because it has to be interpreted only during bash execution. Warning, some implicit variables of nextflow, like (see section 0) cannot be printed easily since it contains $ that should be inactivated.

Uses the exclamation mark ! character as the variable placeholder for Nextflow variables in place of the usual dollar character. Example: process myTask { input: val str from 'Hello', 'Hola', 'Bonjour' shell: ''' echo User $USER says !{str} ''' } !{str} replaced during evaluation, then sent to bash, then $USER replaced. Example: process myTask { input: val str from 'Hello', 'Hola', 'Bonjour' shell: ''' echo User $tempo says !{str} ''' } Bash error message because no tempo variable in the env. Using double quotes: process myTask { input: val str from 'Hello', 'Hola', 'Bonjour' shell: """ echo User $tempo says !{str} """ } Nextflow error message because no tempo variable in nextflow.

https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/config.html?highlight=params#configuration-file When a pipeline script is launched, Nextflow looks for configuration files in multiple locations. Since each configuration file can contain conflicting settings, the sources are ranked to decide which settings to are applied. All possible configuration sources are reported below, listed in order of priority: Parameters specified on the command line (--something value) Parameters provided using the -params-file option Config file specified using the -C my_config option The config file named nextflow.config in the current directory The config file named nextflow.config in the workflow project directory The config file $HOME/.nextflow/config Values defined within the pipeline script itself (e.g. main.nf) When more than one of these ways of specifying configurations are used, they are merged, so that the settings in the first override the same ones that may appear in the second one, and so on. If you want to ignore any default configuration files and use only the custom one use the command line option -C <config file>. Three main sections inside a config file: variables, scopes and directives
Variables can be defined at the begining of the config file 1) variables that will be used in the main.nf file. 2) variables that will be used only in the config file.

Options of singularity: enabled Turn this flag to true to enable Singularity execution (default: false). autoMounts When true Nextflow automatically mounts host paths in the executed container. It requires the user bind control feature enabled in your Singularity installation (default: false). runOptions This attribute can be used to provide any extra command line options supported by the singularity exec. --bind mount a folder point into the container. Mandatory such that singularity is able to understand the tree of the machine used. Example: --bind /pasteur, in order for singularity to access to /pasteur/usr/local for instance. By default, singularity uses --bind $HOME --no-home does not use $HOME (which is what is used by default). Probably create a tmp folder or an empty $HOME. This prevent singularity to use $HOME to look for applications and forces it to use only what is inside the container --home $HOME:/home/$USER to change the $HOME for singularity cacheDir The directory where remote Singularity images are stored. When using a computing cluster it must be a shared folder accessible to all computing nodes. In singularity, there is no entrypoint to manage. Remember that Nextflow use singularity exec and not singularity run (see protocol ).

DrvFs is a filesystem plugin to WSL that was designed to support interop between WSL and the Windows filesystem. DrvFs enables WSL to mount drives with supported file systems under /mnt, such as /mnt/c, /mnt/d, etc. You can learn more about DrvFs and the WSL filesystem in a previous blog post from June 2016, WSL File System Support, which covers the Linux filesystem as it pertains to WSL and compares it to the Windows filesystem.

In order to mount a Windows drive using DrvFs, you can use the regular Linux mount command. For example, to mount a removable drive D: as /mnt/d directory, run the following commands: volum="d" # Warning: never use rm -r sudo mkdir /mnt/$volum sudo mount -r -t drvfs ${volum^^}: /mnt/$volum # -o ro: read only mode # -r: read only mode chmod u=rx,g=rx,o=rx /mnt/$volum #provide an error message that says that the folder is Read-only file system Warning: if D: does not exist in windows, it will return an error (we can only mount what exists). Now, you will be able to access the files of your D: drive under /mnt/d. When you wish to unmount the drive, for example so you can safely remove it, run the following command: sudo umount /mnt/$volum # Warning: never use rm -r # if "target is busy" message, get out of /mnt/$volum (go back to home for instance) Warning: never use rm -r after mkdir /mnt/$volum, because it remove all the distant files ! With: sudo mount -r It is not possible to remove files.

When you wish to mount a network location, you can of course create a mapped network drive in Windows and mount that as indicated above. However, it's also possible to mount them directly using a UNC path: # Warning: never use rm -r sudo mkdir /mnt/share sudo mount -t drvfs '\\zeus.pasteur.fr\BioIT\gmillot' /mnt/share This mount \\zeus.pasteur.fr\BioIT\gmillot into /mnt/share With a variable, use this: FOLDER="\\\zeus.pasteur.fr\BioIT\gmillot" sudo mount -t drvfs "$FOLDER" /mnt/share

New versions of currently installed packages that cannot be upgraded without changing the install status of another package will be left at their current version. The nextflow pipeline file is named by default main.nf. The nextflow config file must are named by default nextflow.config. It is possible to modify these two names. But it will not work if the idea is to work from a distant repository (see section Precision when running a distant nextflow file of protocol 136).

Nextflow create a folder for each process of the .nf file (or each parallelization of each process) in the work directory. For instance, 00/5bf63033e13094f180fe69c583ce3c. Then, everything of the process is performed in this folder, which becomes the working environment (a kind of home). If INPUT is present, then files or values are imported. For the files, a symbolic link is created pointing to the initial file (in another folder of the work directory, or in a dataset folder). All the new files are created here. If publishDir is used, then the files referenced in OUTPUT are copy/paste into the designed publishDir folder.

Warning, because of the symbolic links, every imported file that is modified by the process is not only modified in the work folder but also were the link point, meaning that initial input data can be modifed ! To prevent that: 1) always use input files that are "write" protected (read and execute only). 2) Copy the input file in the process before working: input: file fs script: """ cp ${fs} tempo.txt chmod 777 tempo.txt ... See also section Protection of the initial files if modified in processes for a better example of copy.

A strong advantage of nextflow is to rerun the pipeline using the -resume option of the run command. In such case, all the processes that are cache 'true' are not run but linked to the previous same process execution, which save lots of time! However, all the variables of the .config used in the process must be declared in the input section of the process. Otherwise, nextflow will not rerun a cache 'true' process using a variable modified in the .config file.

The scope of a process is such that if a variable is not in the input section, it looks for variables in the working environment of nextflow, which has notably sourced the env{} environment of the config file. Thus, it is not mandatory to use the input section to declare variables. However, in that case, nextflow will not rerun a cache 'true' process using a variable modified in the .config file.

The -resume option of nextflow has a considerable benefit, as it prevent the running of long processes. For instance, when changing a parameter in the .config file, nextflow will rerun only the processes that is impacted by the change and all the subsequent ones. However, this benefit comes with tricky behaviors that must be anticipated: 1) modification inside a file (see section Protection of the initial files if modified in processes). 2) if the code inside the script section of a process A is unchanged and the input are the same, nextflow uses the last work folder created during the last time that the process A has been run. And Nextflow indicates that process A is "cached". This is the expected behavior. However, if modifications of the script section of a process A, goes back to a previous one (word to word), it seems that Nextflow uses the last work folder created using this previous script. It should be logical. But because of 1), this can generate behaviors difficult to understand. Of note, both the work and .nextflow folders are used by the -resume option. Erasing the work folder is sometimes not sufficient to prevent this option to run. Only the .nextflow deletion will trigger the message: WARN: It appears you have never run this project before -- Option -resume is ignored

Protection of the initial files if modified in processes

If an input file is modified in a process, we could imagine that only the file present in the work directory is modified. But due to the symbolic link, the initial file will be also modified. To prevent this: - NEVER modify a file using the same name. always change the mane of the modified file. - ALWAYS copy these files in the process that modifies the file, not in another process (to optimize the -resume option of nextflow run).
